questions.question: What is the difference between == and === in JavaScript?
questions.title: Double Vs Triple Equals
questions.direct_answer: == (loose) coerces types before comparing ('1' == 1 is true). === (strict) checks type + value with NO coercion ('1' === 1 is false). Always use === — == has 7 coercion rules that cause bugs.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The behavioral difference, verified:

```js
'1' == 1     // true — == coerces the string to a number
'1' === 1    // false — different types, no coercion

null == undefined  // true — the ONE loose match that isn't coercion
null === undefined // false — different types

0 == false   // true — false coerces to 0
0 === false  // false — different types

'' == 0      // true — '' coerces to 0
'' === 0    // false

[] == false  // true — [] → '' → 0
[] === false // false

// The null case (the one == is sometimes useful):
if (value == null) { }  // matches null AND undefined — the only defensible ==
if (value === null || value === undefined) { } // the explicit version
```

== applies the Abstract Equality algorithm: when types differ, it coerces (string → number, boolean → number, object → primitive) before comparing. The coercion rules are 7 dense spec steps — the source of the 'JavaScript is weird' memes.

=== is Strict Equality: same type AND same value, with no coercion. The only exception-like case: NaN !== NaN (NaN is never equal to itself — check with Number.isNaN()).

The industry rule: always ===. The coercion cases == handles are almost always accidental bugs, not intent. The ONE exception: value == null as a shorthand for 'null or undefined' — defensible, though the explicit || form is clearer.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    E1[1 == '1'] →|coerce| TRUE1[true]
    E2[1 === '1'] →|different types| FALSE1[false]
    E3[0 == false] →|false → 0| TRUE2[true]
    E4[0 === false] →|different types| FALSE2[false]
    N[value == null] →|matches both| MATCH[null AND undefined]
    S[always use ===] → SAFE[no coercion surprises]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The Abstract Equality algorithm (=='s rules), summarized: if types match, compare values. If different: null and undefined are mutually equal (the one cross-type pair that isn't coercion). String and number: the string becomes a number. Boolean: the boolean becomes a number, then re-check. Object vs primitive: the object is ToPrimitive'd (valueOf/toString), then the comparison re-runs. After coercion, the values must match exactly.

The coercive chains that produce surprises: [] == false works because [] → '' (its primitive) → 0, and false → 0 — both 0. The chain is spec-correct but no one reasons about it at the keyboard — which is the case for ===.

The Object.is variant (the third comparison, for completeness): like === but treats +0 and -0 as different, and NaN as equal to itself. The use case: Object.is(NaN, NaN) === true — the NaN-safe check that === can't do. Mostly for spec-level operations; day-to-day, === everywhere.
